gloss: A boxer or wrestler in the weight class between lightweight and middleweight.
examples: He won the *welterweight* title in the seventh round.
Two of the best *welterweights* in the country are fighting tonight.
She moved up from lightweight to *welterweight* last season.

gloss: The state of being healthy, comfortable, and happy.
examples: The company says employee *wellbeing* is a priority this year.
Regular exercise improves both physical and mental *wellbeing*.
He worried about his mother's *wellbeing* after the move.

gloss: In stories, a person who turns into a wolf at the full moon.
examples: The movie is about a teenage *werewolf*.
Villagers claimed that *werewolves* hunted in the forest.
He dressed as a *werewolf* for Halloween.

gloss: The direction in which the sun sets, or the region lying in that direction.
examples: Our windows face *west*, so the afternoons are bright.
Storms usually come in from the *west*.
The town lies twenty miles to the *west*.

ru: вестерн (фильм или книга о Диком Западе)
gloss: A movie or book about cowboys and life on the American frontier.
examples: My grandfather watched a *western* every Sunday night.
The theater is showing three classic *westerns* this month.
It's a *western* with a surprising ending.

gloss: A person from Europe or North America, or from the western part of a country.
examples: Few *westerners* had visited the region back then.
As a *westerner*, he found the local customs unfamiliar at first.
The village rarely sees *westerners*.

ru: удар, неприятность (чаще в обороте double whammy — двойной удар)
gloss: A sudden setback or piece of bad luck, most often in the phrase "double whammy".
examples: Rising rent and a pay cut were a double *whammy* for the family.
The storm hit farmers with another *whammy*.
Higher taxes and higher gas prices are a double *whammy* for commuters.

gloss: A whistling sound made when someone has trouble breathing.
examples: The doctor heard a faint *wheeze* in his chest.
She climbed the stairs with a heavy *wheeze*.
The nurse noted *wheezes* in both lungs.

gloss: A long piece of leather or rope on a handle, used to drive animals or to strike.
examples: The driver cracked his *whip* and the horses started forward.
Old *whips* hung on the barn wall.
He never used a *whip* on his horses.

gloss: A neck injury caused when the head is thrown suddenly forward and back.
examples: She suffered *whiplash* when the truck hit her from behind.
He was treated for *whiplash* after the accident.
*Whiplash* can take weeks to heal.

gloss: A spinning current of water that pulls things toward its center.
examples: A *whirlpool* formed where the two rivers met.
Swimmers are warned about *whirlpools* below the dam.
The little boat was caught in a *whirlpool*.

gloss: A column of air spinning quickly across the ground, or a fast and hectic series of events.
examples: A *whirlwind* lifted dust across the empty field.
The past month has been a *whirlwind* of meetings and flights.
Small *whirlwinds* are common out in the desert.

gloss: Very quiet speech made without using the voice.
examples: She answered in a *whisper* so the baby wouldn't wake up.
There were *whispers* about layoffs all week.
His voice dropped to a *whisper*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A cheap white paint made from lime, or an attempt to hide the truth about wrongdoing.
examples: The fence got a fresh coat of *whitewash* every spring.
Critics called the committee's report a *whitewash*.
The barn walls were bright with *whitewash*.

gloss: A complete thing that contains all of its parts.
examples: Two halves make a *whole*.
The report should be judged as a *whole*.
These pieces fit together into a single *whole*.
contrast: The w is silent, so *whole* sounds exactly like *hole*.

gloss: The string in a candle or oil lamp that burns.
examples: Trim the *wick* before you light the candle.
The *wick* burned down into the wax.
These candles have thick cotton *wicks*.

gloss: Thin flexible branches woven together to make furniture and baskets.
examples: The porch has two chairs made of *wicker*.
She keeps the towels in a basket of white *wicker*.
*Wicker* cracks if you leave it out in the rain.

gloss: Nature away from towns and farms, where animals live free.
examples: These birds are rarely seen in the *wild*.
The cubs were released back into the *wild*.
Fewer than a thousand of them survive in the *wild*.

gloss: The quality of being ready and glad to do something.
examples: Her *willingness* to help impressed the whole team.
He showed no *willingness* to compromise.
Success here depends on a *willingness* to learn.

gloss: An informal word for someone who is weak or easily frightened.
examples: Don't be such a *wimp* — the water's fine.
He called his brother a *wimp* for backing out.
The coach has no patience for *wimps*.

gloss: A machine with a turning drum that pulls a rope or cable to lift or drag heavy things.
examples: The truck pulled the car out of the ditch with a *winch*.
Sailors used a *winch* to raise the anchor.
Both *winches* on the deck need repair.

gloss: A sudden amount of money that you did not expect to receive.
examples: The settlement brought the town a two-million-dollar *windfall*.
She used the *windfall* to pay off her student loans.
Oil companies enjoyed record *windfalls* that year.

gloss: A pilot who flies beside and protects the lead plane, or informally a friend who backs you up socially.
examples: The captain lost contact with his *wingman* over the ocean.
He brought his roommate along as his *wingman*.
The two *wingmen* stayed close to the formation.

gloss: A quick closing of one eye as a friendly or joking signal.
examples: He gave her a *wink* and walked away.
She agreed with a smile and a *wink*.
The joke ended with a *wink* at the audience.

gloss: A secret, usually court-approved, connection used to listen to someone's phone calls.
examples: Agents got a warrant for a *wiretap* on his office phone.
*Wiretaps* recorded hours of conversation.
Evidence from the *wiretap* was thrown out by the judge.

gloss: A thin, delicate piece or streak of something such as smoke, cloud, or hair.
examples: A *wisp* of smoke rose from the chimney.
*Wisps* of hair escaped from under her hat.
There wasn't a *wisp* of cloud in the sky.

gloss: Money that an employer takes out of a paycheck and sends to the government as tax.
examples: Federal *withholding* comes out of every paycheck.
You can change your *withholding* by filing a new W-4.
Too little *withholding* means a big bill in April.

gloss: A trouble or misfortune, often used in the plural for a run of problems.
examples: The team's *woes* continued with a third straight loss.
Rising costs added to the airline's financial *woes*.
She listened patiently to his tale of *woe*.

gloss: A musical instrument such as a flute, clarinet, or oboe that you play by blowing.
examples: The clarinet is her favorite *woodwind*.
The *woodwinds* sit in front of the brass section.
He plays three different *woodwinds*.

gloss: Someone who works far too much and finds it hard to stop.
examples: My father was a *workaholic* who never took vacations.
The firm is full of *workaholics*.
She admits she's a bit of a *workaholic*.

gloss: A person or machine that does a lot of steady, reliable work.
examples: That old truck has been the *workhorse* of the farm for years.
He's the quiet *workhorse* of the department.
These printers are the *workhorses* of the office.

gloss: The area where a person works, or an area on a computer screen set up for one project.
examples: She cleared her *workspace* before starting the drawings.
The office has shared *workspaces* instead of private rooms.
Each project opens in its own *workspace*.

ru: рабочее место с компьютером, рабочая станция
gloss: A desk with a computer and the equipment for one worker.
examples: Every *workstation* has two monitors.
He logged in at an empty *workstation*.
The lab added six new *workstations* this fall.

gloss: The earth and everyone on it, or a particular area of life and activity.
examples: News of the discovery traveled around the *world*.
She wanted to see the *world* before settling down.
The *world* of professional sports can be brutal.

gloss: A person who takes part in a religious service or prays to a god.
examples: Hundreds of *worshipers* filled the church.
A lone *worshiper* knelt near the altar.
*Worshipers* gathered outside the mosque before dawn.
contrast: American English spells it with one p, *worshiper*; British English uses *worshipper*.

gloss: The value or importance of something or someone.
examples: The painting's *worth* has doubled since 1990.
He wanted to prove his *worth* to the team.
Her net *worth* is listed in the report.

gloss: Paper or plastic used to cover something, especially a gift or a product.
examples: Tear off the *wrapping* and see what's inside.
She saves the *wrapping* from every present.
The candy comes in gold *wrapping*.
contrast: The w in wr- is silent: RAP-ing.

gloss: Very great anger, especially of someone powerful.
examples: He feared the *wrath* of his father.
The decision brought down the *wrath* of the neighbors.
She faced the full *wrath* of the press.
contrast: Silent w; Americans say RATH with the vowel of *bath*, the British say ROTH.

gloss: A band of cloth, rubber, or leather worn around the wrist.
examples: Every guest got a paper *wristband* at the gate.
He wears a rubber *wristband* for the charity.
Runners pick up their *wristbands* at check-in.

gloss: An official written order issued by a court.
examples: His lawyers filed a *writ* of habeas corpus.
The court issued a *writ* ordering the records released.
Several *writs* were served the same morning.
contrast: Silent w and a short vowel: *writ* rhymes with *sit*, not with *write*.

gloss: The activity of putting words on paper or a screen, or the words themselves.
examples: His *writing* has improved a lot this year.
I can't read her *writing*.
Please put your request in *writing*.

gloss: Illegal or dishonest behavior.
examples: The company denied any *wrongdoing*.
The audit found no evidence of *wrongdoing*.
He resigned but admitted no *wrongdoing*.

gloss: A colorless gas used in very bright lamps and camera flashes.
examples: The headlights use *xenon* instead of ordinary bulbs.
*Xenon* is one of the noble gases.
The lamp is filled with *xenon* at low pressure.
contrast: The x is pronounced like z: ZEE-nahn.

gloss: Fear or hatred of people from other countries.
examples: The campaign was criticized for stirring up *xenophobia*.
*Xenophobia* rose sharply after the attacks.
Teachers talked with students about racism and *xenophobia*.
contrast: The x sounds like z: zen-uh-FOH-bee-uh.

gloss: The tissue in a plant that carries water up from the roots.
examples: Water moves through the *xylem* to the leaves.
The diagram labels the *xylem* and the phloem.
*Xylem* cells are hollow when they are mature.
contrast: The x is pronounced like z: ZY-luhm.

gloss: An involuntary opening of the mouth when you are tired or bored.
examples: She covered a *yawn* with her hand.
His speech produced a few *yawns* in the back row.
A long *yawn* told me it was time for bed.

gloss: The unit of money used in Japan.
examples: The ticket cost eight thousand *yen*.
The *yen* fell against the dollar this week.
He changed his dollars into *yen* at the airport.
contrast: The plural takes no -s: *five hundred yen*.

gloss: The unit of money used in China.
examples: The meal cost about sixty *yuan*.
The *yuan* has weakened slightly this month.
Prices are listed in both dollars and *yuan*.

gloss: Great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or a goal.
examples: She attacked the project with surprising *zeal*.
His reforming *zeal* made him enemies on the council.
The volunteers worked with real *zeal*.

gloss: A person with extreme, uncompromising beliefs, especially religious or political ones.
examples: He was dismissed as a *zealot* by his own party.
A handful of *zealots* disrupted the meeting.
The movement attracted both idealists and *zealots*.
contrast: Though it comes from *zeal* (ZEEL), *zealot* has a short vowel: ZEL-uht.

gloss: The highest point something reaches, or the point in the sky directly overhead.
examples: The band was at its *zenith* in the late seventies.
The sun reaches its *zenith* around noon.
His career hit its *zenith* with that trial.

gloss: The band of twelve star signs used in astrology.
examples: Which sign of the *zodiac* were you born under?
The ceiling was painted with symbols of the *zodiac*.
Her column explains the *zodiac* sign by sign.

gloss: In horror stories, a dead body brought back to life and able to walk.
examples: The show is about survivors of a *zombie* outbreak.
*Zombies* shuffled toward the fence.
After two nights without sleep I felt like a *zombie*.

gloss: An area set apart by a particular purpose, rule, or quality.
examples: Parking is not allowed in the loading *zone*.
The city divided the area into three residential *zones*.
Slow down — you're in a school *zone*.

gloss: Tiny animals that drift in the sea and are eaten by fish and whales.
examples: Whales filter *zooplankton* out of the water.
Warmer water has reduced the *zooplankton* in the bay.
The samples were full of *zooplankton*.

gloss: The single cell formed when an egg and a sperm join.
examples: The *zygote* begins to divide within hours.
Every human being starts as a single *zygote*.
The lab studied *zygotes* under a microscope.
